title: Samaria Under Siege and Hezekiah in Jerusalem
lead: A situation that seems hopeless can change in a single day, and no enemy is greater than God.
questions: What letter do you read over and over at night instead of spreading it out before the LORD, and what good news are you keeping quiet about while the city next door is starving?
In what matter have you declared in advance that there will be no miracle, and how, then, are you different from the officer at the gate?
Who at the gate, on the margins of your world, should you start listening to, since that is exactly the way good news likes to come in?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Two besieged cities, one lesson: sometimes, with God, a single night separates “there’s no way out” from “it’s all over.” The text describes the siege of Samaria with a price list of despair: a donkey’s head for eighty shekels, mothers striking a bargain beyond anything the mind can hold. Into this hopeless situation Elisha throws a promise that is boldly specific: “About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel.” The king’s officer scoffed, “even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?” and heard in reply: “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it.” Unbelief did not stop the miracle; it only stopped the unbeliever from sharing in it. God entrusted the good news to four lepers at the gate, who discovered the empty camp of the Arameans, driven off by the Lord with the sound of chariots. What they said could weigh on the conscience of many a congregation: “Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent” (WEB). Evangelism in its purest form: one hungry person telling another where they found bread.

Several generations later Sennacherib stands before Jerusalem, conqueror of forty-six cities of Judah. The ransom did not help, and the Rabshakeh wages psychological warfare beneath the walls: Egypt is a splintered reed, and the LORD? Isn’t He the One whose high places Hezekiah removed? An accusation cut from the cloth of the king’s own reform. Hezekiah, who had already done everything that was his to do, now does what has become a model of prayer for three thousand years: he takes the blackmail letter, goes up to the temple, and spreads it out before the LORD. He does not deny the facts: it is true, Assyria has laid waste the nations. He simply sets them before a greater fact: those gods were only wood and stone, while “You made the heavens and the earth.” He does not pray for himself: “so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.”

“And that very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.” An inscription survives in which Sennacherib boasts that he shut Hezekiah up “like a bird in a cage.” Of the capture of Jerusalem there is not a word, because it never happened. The enemy’s record falls silent at exactly the point where the Bible speaks of deliverance.

We close the section on coming to the end of our strength with the stories of two besieged cities several generations apart: Samaria, strangled by famine under the Arameans, and Jerusalem, surrounded by the Assyrian war machine. Two stories, one lesson: with God, sometimes exactly one night passes between “there’s no way out” and “it’s all over.”

sections.heading: A Price List of Despair
paragraphs: The text reports the siege of Samaria by way of a price list, and it is more terrifying than many a battle scene. A donkey’s head, an unclean animal no Israelite would touch in normal times, “sold for eighty shekels of silver,” a small fortune. A quarter cab of dove’s dung, whether fuel or the last substitute for food, went for five shekels. And the narrator adds one more scene that is hard to read: two mothers agreed to eat their sons, and one of them kept the bargain. Hearing this, the king tears his clothes, and the people see that underneath, next to his skin, he is wearing sackcloth. It is a haunting detail: piety worn under the clothes, private austerity without public repentance and without a change of course. That kind of religion does not save a city. The king immediately shows what it is worth, because instead of seeking God he swears to cut off Elisha’s head. His messenger speaks the sentence that marks rock bottom in this story: “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” Here is a man who has stopped waiting. It happens to us too: a theologically correct diagnosis with nothing left in it but resignation.

sections.heading: About This Time Tomorrow
paragraphs: Elisha’s answer is specific to the point of audacity: “About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel.” Tomorrow. Not “someday,” not “once you repent.” Twenty-four hours from the specter of starvation to cheap bread. The king’s officer reacts the way most of us probably would: “Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?” The prophet answers with words that should stand as a footnote to every cynical remark: “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it.” Unbelief did not stop the miracle: it happened on schedule, and the prediction came true to the shekel. Unbelief stopped only one thing: the unbeliever’s share in the miracle. The next day, trampled in the gateway by the crowd rushing for food, the officer saw everything and ate nothing. The skeptic in this story is right about one thing: humanly speaking, it really was impossible. Only no one was talking about human possibilities.

sections.heading: Four Lepers
paragraphs: The most beautiful thing in this story is whom God entrusted with the good news. Not the king, not the elders, not even the prophet. Four lepers barely surviving at the gate, shut out of the city and out of hope. Their math was simple: in the city, famine; by the walls, death; in the enemy camp, maybe death, and maybe not. “Why just sit here until we die?” At twilight they went to the camp of the Arameans, and there was no one there, because the LORD had made the besiegers hear the rumble of chariots and the thunder of a great army, so they fled in panic, leaving everything behind. The four outcasts walked into the empty camp and felt as if they were dreaming: they ate, they drank, they carried off silver and hid it. Then one of them says the sentence that ought to be read at every mission conference: “We aren’t doing right. Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent” (WEB). They went and woke the city. This is evangelism in its purest form, before it gets overgrown with programs and strategies: one hungry person telling another hungry person where they found bread. The people kept outside the gate became the first heralds of rescue for those who had kept them there. God takes particular delight in entrusting His best news to people outside the boundaries we set, and a community that does not listen to voices from the margins can sleep right through its own rescue. The king very nearly missed it: he smelled a trap in the good news and sent out scouts. The road to the Jordan was littered with discarded clothing and equipment. It was all true.

sections.heading: A Great King Before a Small City
paragraphs: Several generations later, a power of an entirely different caliber stands beneath the walls of Jerusalem. This is Sennacherib, ruler of Assyria, the empire that had just wiped northern Israel off the map and captured forty-six fortified cities of Judah. Hezekiah first tried the road we all know: pay them to leave you alone. He handed over three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold; he even stripped the gold from the doors of the temple. It did not help, because a blackmailer who has been fed comes back hungrier. An Assyrian dignitary, the Rabshakeh, comes up to the walls and takes his stand, as the text notes, “by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field.” That is exactly the spot where, a generation earlier, the prophet Isaiah had stood before King Ahaz, Hezekiah’s father, and urged him to trust God, not Assyria. Ahaz refused. Now his son, in the same place, is asked the same question: whom do you trust?

In fairness, we must add that Hezekiah was no dreamer sitting on his hands waiting for a miracle. The book mentions that he brought water into the city. To this day you can walk through the tunnel cut in the rock by which he channeled the Gihon spring to a pool inside the walls, so that besieged Jerusalem would have water to drink and the besiegers would not. He strengthened the walls, stockpiled weapons, organized the defense. And then, having done everything that was his to do, he entrusted the whole matter to God. The Bible sees no conflict between sensible preparation and trust; the conflict it knows is between trust and a panicked search for rescue anywhere but in the Almighty. The tunnel did not save Jerusalem. But it was dug by a man who knew that rescue would come from above anyway.

sections.heading: Propaganda Beneath the Walls
paragraphs: The Rabshakeh’s speech is a masterpiece of psychological warfare that sounds disturbingly modern. He speaks loudly, in Hebrew, over the heads of the diplomats, straight to the people on the wall. He knocks out every support in turn. Egypt is “that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it.” And the LORD? Here comes an argument diabolical in its cleverness: “is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed”? The accusation is cut from the cloth of the king’s own reform: the cleansing of worship presented as an attack on piety. Anyone who has ever set something in order in God’s house knows this accusation firsthand. Finally, the ultimate taunt: no god of any nation has saved his land from Assyria, so how would the LORD be any different? The living God lumped together with the idols of the defeated. Even the offer of surrender is dressed in the language of paradise: “a land of grain and new wine… so that you may live and not die.” Deportation wrapped up as a sales brochure. And the people, at the king’s command, “remained silent and did not answer a word.” Sometimes that is the wisest thing to do with mockery: not to argue with it on its own terms, but to take it higher.

sections.heading: A Letter Spread Out Before the LORD
paragraphs: That is exactly what Hezekiah does. He tears his clothes and goes into the house of the LORD, and when Sennacherib sends a second delegation, this time in writing, the king does something that has become a model of prayer for three thousand years: he “received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD.” He physically laid the blackmail document open before God, because it was God who had been insulted in it. Hezekiah prays a prayer in which he himself stops being the subject. He does not deny the facts: “Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste these nations and their lands.” Faith does not mean denying reality. It means setting it before a greater reality: those gods were “only wood and stone,” “the work of human hands,” while “You made the heavens and the earth.” The closing request is not “save us because we are afraid,” but: “so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.” Each of us sometimes gets our own letter from Sennacherib: a diagnosis, a layoff notice, a letter that makes our knees buckle. We can read it over and over through the night. Or we can spread it out before the LORD and hand the matter higher.

sections.heading: One Night
paragraphs: The answer comes through Isaiah: the king of Assyria “will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it.” And then a single sentence: “And that very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.” By morning, all that was left of the great power was a camp of corpses. The city that in the evening had been “a bird in a cage” woke up free, and not one of its defenders had shot a single arrow. Sennacherib slunk back to Nineveh, where years later his own sons killed him, and in the temple of his god at that, in the place that should have been the safest of all. The God who had been mocked beneath the walls of Jerusalem defended His city; the god before whom Sennacherib knelt at home could not save his own worshiper in his own house. The text leaves this contrast without comment, because none is needed. History has added an ironic footnote here: an Assyrian inscription survives in which Sennacherib boasts of capturing forty-six cities of Judah and of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage.” He lists everything. About the capture of Jerusalem he says not a word, because he had nothing to boast about. The enemy’s boastful record falls silent at exactly the point where the Bible speaks of deliverance.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Each of us takes something different from these two besieged cities today. If you are in a situation you have already priced like Samaria, by the price list of despair, hear God’s promise: “about this time tomorrow.” It is sometimes closer than your forecast reaches, and the only thing that can shut you out of the miracle is a certainty, declared in advance, that there won’t be one. If you have received your own letter from Sennacherib, do not write back to the mocker. Spread the letter out before the Lord, call the facts by their name, and set them before the Almighty. For us as a community, this story holds two lessons. First: good news likes to enter the city through the gate where the excluded sit; whoever does not listen to people on the margins risks missing the rescue. Second: in this story we ourselves are the four lepers. We have found a camp full of bread we did not win. If we keep quiet about it, we are not doing right, because this day is a day of good news.
